summary:
Lambayeque has no trans-specific ordinance, municipal rule or documented pattern of local enforcement on record; a trans visitor in this department is bound throughout by Peru's national framework. Trans identity is not criminalised in Peru, so being trans is not itself an offence. The operative constraints are the national restriction on shared public facilities, the absence of hate-crime coverage for LGBT people in the Penal Code, and a documented level of violence against trans women.

The facility restriction was adopted in stages during 2025. On 20 February 2025 the congressional Comision de Mujer y Familia approved by unanimity a dictamen merging bills 6506 and 8457, sponsored by Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Munante, prohibiting any person from entering a public sanitary facility designated for the sex opposite to their birth sex, with narrow exceptions covering custody and situations where presence is required, such as accompanying minors, elderly people or people with disabilities; the text would also oblige venues not to post ambiguous restroom signs. At that date the text still required plenary backing. On 2 April 2025 the plenary of Congress approved the dictamen and waived a second vote on the 'Ley que fortalece el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los ninos y adolescentes', whose Article 5.1 carries the prohibition. Infobae Peru reports the trigger as a July 2023 complaint about gendered restroom labels at Lima's Jorge Chavez international airport.

The restriction reaches ordinary venues in Lambayeque as it does anywhere in Peru, and its enforcement would rest on security staff checking the national identity document to decide whether a woman entering a women's restroom is trans or cisgender, according to activist Gianna Camacho, quoted by Infobae Peru. A consumer-protection body has already declined to intervene on the same logic: SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against the gym chain SmartFit, which assigned restroom use to the sex recorded in her identity document.

Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the hate-crime provisions of the new Penal Code, and the state's crime-registration systems do not incorporate sexual orientation or gender identity, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such. Assault against a trans visitor would therefore be charged as ordinary assault.

Violence against trans people is recorded at national level and the figures are substantial. The annual report of the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia records 54 assassinations of LGBTI people and 170 rights-violation cases between 2020 and 2023; the homicide victims were 30 trans women, 23 gay men and one lesbian. Nineteen killings occurred in 2023 alone, 12 of them trans women, and the killers were not identified in 26 of the 54 homicides, including 13 of the 19 in 2023. In February 2023 Rubi Torres Silvano, a 31-year-old trans sex worker, was kidnapped from central Lima by the 'Los Gallegos' extortion gang and shot some 30 times in Carabayllo, days after Priscila Aguado Huatuco was shot; two killers were arrested in March 2023.
tangentialFactors:
The facility provision is contested on constitutional grounds. In a legal analysis of 15 April 2025 by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte, the human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru reads Article 5 as a direct breach of equality and non-discrimination under Article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and Article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights, resting on the stereotype that trans people are more prone to enter restrooms in order to harass or sexually abuse minors. The institute has also recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu.

Peru's position sits against the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, which held that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. On hate-crime coverage, the 2017 repeal left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

One protective case is on record. In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan Leon, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marin, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history, reaching the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

Two further protective developments are documented. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are also constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people. On television, presenter Ana Maria Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.
localsOnly:
Gender-identity recognition in Peru remains long, costly and invasive, which shapes how residents obtain documents matching their gender before the restroom rule is applied to them at all.

Resident complaints have limited reach. SPC-INDECOPI Resolution 0735-2022 dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against SmartFit, where the company grounded bathroom assignment on the sex recorded in the DNI, and the same consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's complaint against a gym that enforced the 2025 policy.

The state has not incorporated sexual orientation or gender identity into its crime-registration systems, so hate crimes cannot be prosecuted as such by residents reporting to police. National monitoring for residents comes from the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI at Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia, whose tally covers 170 rights-violation cases alongside the 54 killings recorded between 2020 and 2023, with Gianna Camacho, a trans journalist and human-rights defender, stressing that published figures are only a sub-registry.

In healthcare settings residents face a changed standard rather than a uniformly improved one: June 2024 guidance removed pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health documents.
outOfScopeNotes:
All three sources address the national framework and contain no Lambayeque-specific content. Municipal bylaws in Chiclayo or other districts of the department, regional police practice, and departmental violence figures are therefore unresolved rather than absent, and no claim is made about them here.

Whether venues in Lambayeque in fact check identity documents at restroom doors is not documented in any source. The enforcement mechanism described comes from an activist's assessment of how the rule would operate, not from observed practice in this department.

The inventory supplies national homicide and rights-violation figures for 2020-2023 only. Totals for 2024 and 2025, and any Lambayeque share of those totals, are not sourced.

Whether any discrimination complaint arising in Lambayeque has been received or dismissed by INDECOPI or by the health authorities is not sourced, and the outcome of constitutional challenges to the April 2025 law beyond the July 2025 ruling on a separate decree is unresolved.
